disclaimer: Historical records of observed natural events on Mars. Not current weather, not a forecast, not a hazard model. Estimates are marked. Events outside Jezero/Gale are context-only and must be labeled as such. Local event positions are crater-level context only; their relation to the app's DTM footprints is not verified, so do not render them as exact map pins.

events.date_note: Storm appeared Jan 1, 2022 (Mars 2020 mission; the NASA blog dates Ingenuity Flight 19's original slot to Jan 5, 2022 = Sol 313). Storm dissipated within the following weeks; Flight 19 flew no earlier than Jan 23, 2022.
events.location: Jezero Crater region (regional storm encompassing the crater; crater-level context, not an exact pin)
events.summary: Strong regional dust storm, the earliest in the Mars year the team had seen one of this strength. MEDA measured ~7% air-density drop; sunlight absorbed by Ingenuity's solar array fell ~18%. Ingenuity Flight 19 was delayed - the first flight delay due to weather on another world.

events.location: Jezero Crater floor, at the rover's position (crater-level context)
events.summary: First-ever recorded sounds of a Martian dust devil: a dust devil passed directly over Perseverance during a swarm across the crater floor; the SuperCam microphone and MEDA captured it.
events.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech; Murdoch et al., Nature Communications 2022

events.location: Thorofare Ridge area, western rim of Jezero Crater (crater-level context; relation to app DTM footprint not verified)
events.summary: ~60 m-wide dust devil imaged moving east-to-west at ~19 kph, about 4 km from the rover. Height estimated ~2 km from its shadow (top out of frame).

events.location: Witch Hazel Hill area, western rim of Jezero Crater (crater-level context; relation to app DTM footprint not verified)
events.summary: A ~65 m-wide dust devil imaged consuming a trailing ~5 m-wide one from about 1 km away; two more dust devils visible in the background.

events.date_note: Storm grew over weeks and was declared planet-encircling by the MARCI team around Jun 17-20, 2018. Date given is Sol 2082 (Jun 15, 2018), when Curiosity took its hazy self-portrait.
events.location: Gale Crater (observed in-situ by Curiosity; crater-level context)
events.summary: Planet-encircling dust event. Tau (atmospheric opacity) at Gale exceeded 8.0, the highest the MSL mission ever recorded; Mastcam images show the sky darkening over ~2 weeks and the light turning cherry-red between Sol 2058 (May 21) and Sol 2084 (Jun 17).

events.location: Inside Gale Crater, seen from Curiosity's position (crater-level context)
events.summary: Navcam sequence of a dust devil crossing the ground inside Gale Crater on a local summer afternoon.

events.location: Detected by InSight's seismometer at Elysium Planitia (detector location, not the epicenter). Later analysis placed the epicenter close to but outside the Cerberus Fossae region, over 2000 km from the lander. NOT at Jezero or Gale.
events.summary: Largest quake ever detected on another planet. Initial mission estimate: magnitude 5 (NASA, May 2022). Peer-reviewed analysis (Kawamura et al., Geophysical Research Letters, Dec 2022) revised it to magnitude 4.7, with waves lasting ~10 hours and surface waves circling the planet multiple times.
estimated_fields: epicenter (later analysis, close to but outside Cerberus Fossae)

events.location: Detected by InSight at Elysium Planitia (detector location; the source does not fix an epicenter). NOT at Jezero or Gale.
events.summary: InSight's first likely marsquake: the first recorded seismic signal attributable to Mars itself.

events.location: Amazonis Planitia. NOT at Jezero or Gale.
events.summary: Meteoroid estimated 5-12 m wide struck Mars, forming a ~150 m-wide, ~21 m-deep crater with ejecta to ~37 km and exposing boulder-size buried water ice, the closest to the equator ever seen at the time. InSight recorded the magnitude-4 quake; MRO before/after imaging (crater first spotted Feb 11, 2022) confirmed the cause.

events.location: North polar scarp at the edge of the north polar layered deposits (~83.7 N, 235.8 E, from the HiRISE observation metadata). NOT at Jezero or Gale.
events.summary: HiRISE caught at least four avalanches/debris falls in action off a ~700 m-tall scarp during northern spring; dust/ice clouds ~180 m across. First active falls ever imaged on Mars. Trigger unknown - the source lists frost loss, thermal stress, a marsquake or an impact as possibilities; do not assert a cause.

bounded_absences: This is a bounded record set from the cited sources, not an exhaustive catalog of Mars events.
The sources describe Martian dust devils as much weaker and generally smaller than Earth tornadoes; no event in these records matches tornado or hurricane strength.
No seismometer has operated at Jezero or Gale, so no local marsquake records exist for either workspace. InSight seismic records are Elysium Planitia detections, context only.
